title: Seagrass coiled table basket
subtitle: Basketry: a coiled seagrass basket for a fruit bowl or table storage
excerpt: A coiled seagrass basket with a flat base and straight sides, made from natural seagrass rope and bound with natural raffia. Coiled basketry uses a thick rope core that is stitched together in an ascending spiral; seagrass and raffia are the most accessible materials for a first coiled piece. No soaking required.
sourceNotes: Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the coiled basketry technique with rope core; Cassell's Book of the Household (1890) for the seagrass coiling method.

glossaryTerms.definition: A basket construction technique where a thick core material (rope, rush, or bundled grass) is coiled in a flat spiral and stitched to adjacent coils to build up the walls.
Twisted rope made from dried Posidonia or similar marine grass. Available from craft suppliers in natural tan colour. Stiff enough to hold shape in a coil without soaking.
Flat natural strips from the raffia palm, used as the binding thread in coiled basketry. Wraps around and through the coil to stitch adjacent rows together.

content.text: basket is structurally different from a woven willow basket, instead of weaving rods through upright stakes, you coil a rope and stitch adjacent coils together. The technique is simpler to start than willow weaving: no soaking, no staking up, no waling. The base and sides are built in one continuous spiral from the centre outward and upward.
rope as the core and natural
as the binding thread. Both are available from craft suppliers. The finished basket is about 28 cm diameter and 12 cm tall, a generous fruit bowl or kitchen table storage.
About 30 m of 6 mm seagrass rope.
A large hank of natural raffia.
Bodkin for making holes in the coils for stitching.

Thread a length of raffia onto the bodkin. Fold the tip of the seagrass rope back on itself to make a tight spiral start about 4 cm diameter. Stitch the folded start together by wrapping the raffia tightly around both layers of rope several times, then threading the bodkin through the centre of the fold to lock the start.

Continue coiling the seagrass around the central start, stitching each new row to the previous row as you go. The stitch: wrap the raffia three times around the new coil, then drive the bodkin through the previous coil and pull through. Stitch every 15, 20 mm. Keep the base flat, if it starts to dome, push it firmly down on a flat surface and continue.

Once the base reaches 28 cm diameter, begin building up the sides: instead of placing each new coil next to the previous one on the flat, place it on top. The stitch is identical. The walls rise naturally as each coil is placed slightly inward of the previous one's outer edge. Keep the walls vertical by checking from the side every three or four rows.

When the sides reach 12 cm, taper the rope end over the last 10 cm by cutting away the twisted strands of the seagrass with secateurs, leaving the core thin enough to lay flat against the previous coil. Stitch the tapered end down firmly with several close wraps of raffia, then stitch the tip through the coil twice to lock. Trim the raffia flush.
Small pot with lid: make two shallow bowls and place them rim-to-rim.
Coloured accent: use dyed raffia for every third stitch row.

attrs.symptom: The base develops a bowl shape instead of staying flat
attrs.cause: Stitches on the outer edge of the base are pulling the rim inward, doming the base
attrs.fix: When stitching the base, pull the raffia through the previous coil from the inside outward rather than from the outside inward, this changes the direction of tension. Press the base flat on a heavy book between sessions.
